1.pericope_label: I saw a new heaven and a new earth, and there was no more sea

schools.summary: Gill refuses the reading which places this vision in the apostles' own time, when the old Jewish order gave way to a new dispensation; death did not then cease, having reigned ever since, and instead of sorrow and sighing fleeing away there was for three hundred years scarce anything else.

Henry thinks it safest to understand the heavenly state, and reads the new earth as a condition for the bodies of men as the new heaven is for their souls; this world is not newly created but newly opened, and the very earth of the saints, their glorified bodies, will be spiritual and heavenly, suited to those bright mansions.

Clarke reports the rabbinic expectation that God would renew the heavens and the earth at the end of seven thousand years, then refuses to speculate, quoting Calmet that to pretend to say what this new heaven and new earth are, and what their ornaments and qualities, is the greatest of all presumptions; on the sea he supposes it was made new with the rest and probably differently placed. Wesley puts the vision after the resurrection and the general judgment, insists that John is not describing a flourishing state of the church but a new and eternal state of all things, and notices that the verb here is milder than the one used three verses later, since death and mourning and sorrow go away altogether while the former heaven and earth only pass away.

Ellicott takes the governing word apart, since Greek has two words for new, one relating to time and the other to quality, and it is the second which is used throughout this book; the newness pictured is therefore the newness of freshness, so that all things may be new and yet not strange, there being some correspondency between the old and the new. On the sea he finds it strange that so many commentators treat the ornaments of the city as symbolical while taking its annihilation as literal, and recalls how the sea has served the symbolism of the book. Robertson agrees on the method but differs on the scope, since this is not a picture of the renovation of this earth but of the disappearance of this earth and sky, though not of the heaven where God dwells. Barnes sets the whole chapter out as one picture, the redeemed after the judgment drawn under the image of a beautiful city with no temple, for it is all a temple, and needing no light, for God is its light.

debates.question: How literally should the vanishing of the sea be taken?

positions.position: the spiritual teaching is what matters; the sea has been the symbol of restless evil throughout the book
a stern and glorious reality lies behind the symbol, but this earth and sky do disappear
the sea was made new with the rest, and probably differently placed and distributed

themes: the first heaven and the first earth are passed away
the newness of freshness rather than of recent making
and there was no more sea

2.pericope_label: The holy city coming down from God: the tabernacle of God is with men

schools.summary: Gill takes the city for the whole body of the elect rather than the militant church, the general assembly and church of the firstborn, and calls them holy in a sense not yet true, since they will be perfectly holy in themselves, without the being of sin in them or any spot of it upon them.

Clarke reports the rabbinic form of the same expectation, that tabernacle and temple and Jerusalem came down from heaven, the Jewish opinion being that these subsist in spiritual representatives and so cannot be destroyed; on the promise about death he argues that death cannot be destroyed merely by there being no further dying, but only by a general resurrection, so this promise both assures the resurrection and proves that after it death will not return. Wesley adds that the city belongs neither to this world nor to the millennium but to eternity, and is caught in the very act of descending, and takes the clause about death as full proof that the description belongs not to time but to eternity.

Robertson quotes Swete that the new earth must have a new metropolis, not another Babylon but a greater Jerusalem, notes that the title wife is proleptic since the marriage is not yet a reality, and traces the tabernacle metaphor back to the Shekinah glory of the old tent. Barnes insists the descent cannot be pressed, since a city three hundred and seventy miles high with single pearls for gates cannot literally settle on the earth, and measures the promise about tears against a world where no one rises in the morning certain he may not end the day in grief. Ellicott makes the direction of movement the point, since she is seen not rising out of earth or sea like the foes of righteousness but coming down from heaven, the world never evolving a golden age of itself; he marks the change of preposition, God having tabernacled over his people in an earlier chapter and with them here, and counts the negatives that follow as heralds of positive peace.

themes: prepared as a bride adorned for her husband
behold, the tabernacle of God is with men
no sea, no tears, no death, no mourning, no crying, no pain

5.pericope_label: Behold, I make all things new: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end

schools.summary: Gill weighs the Father against Christ as the speaker and leans to Christ, since the speaker calls himself Alpha and Omega as Christ does elsewhere, and it is he who gives thirsty souls the water of life; on the declaration that all is done he fills out the list, since the whole election of grace is completed and every vessel of mercy called, and what was finished on the cross by way of impetration is now done as to application.

Clarke shows the same expectation among the rabbins, who counted the fountain of the world to come among the blessings of a future state, and imagined the lost crying, Wo to us, what good have we lost. Wesley agrees that an angel gives the order to write, thinks the apostle had ceased writing, overcome with ecstasy at the voice of him that spake, takes the second half of the title as explaining the first, and observes that to overcome is more than to thirst; on the verbs he adds a grammarian's caution, that shall and will are one word in both Hebrew and Greek.

Barnes treats the title as decisive, making it morally certain that the speaker is the Lord Jesus and proving him divine, and hears an echo of the cross in the declaration that it is done. Robertson reads it as the first time since the opening chapter that God speaks directly, notes that the message is addressed to the entire world of the blessed rather than to John, suspects a change of speakers in the command to write, and divides the title so that the beginning is the First Cause and the end the Finality. Ellicott would render the promise as a present, I am making all things new, hears the assurance of the Throned One who has presided over all the changing scenes of earth's history, counts the assurance trebly sure with Bengel's note that the book says it is done twice, and finds in the title the ground of the offer to the thirsty, since he who begins the good work will perform it.

debates.question: Who is speaking from the throne?

positions.position: Christ, since the speaker takes the title Alpha and Omega and gives the water of life
God, who here speaks directly for the first time since the opening chapter, though an angel gives the command to write

themes: behold, I make all things new; write, for these words are faithful and true
I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely
he that overcometh shall inherit these things

8.pericope_label: But the fearful, and unbelieving, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake

schools.summary: Gill will not let the first name touch the timorous sheep and lambs of Christ, who are often of a fearful heart on account of sin and temptation, but only those of cowardly spirits who are not valiant for the truth, and who through fear of men either make no profession or drop the one they made lest they be exposed to persecution.

Clarke describes the same men historically, as those who for fear of losing life or property refused a religion they were convinced was true, or fell away when it grew dangerous; he defines the sorcerers as persons who by drugs, philtres and fumigations pretend to produce supernatural effects, and the idolaters as those who offer any kind of worship to anything but God, and is strictest on the liars, taking in every one who speaks contrary to the truth while knowing it and even the man who speaks truth meaning to deceive. He adds that about thirty excellent manuscripts insert sinners into the list, on which evidence Griesbach admitted the word. Wesley disposes of three together, since fornication, sorcery and idolatry generally went in company.

Barnes sets the fearful expressly against the overcomer of the verse before, derives the word for the abominable from a verb meaning to excite disgust, and takes the last term to cover all who are false in their statements, promises and contracts. Robertson makes the second epithet mean untrustworthy rather than merely unbelieving, set against Christ who is called the faithful, adds that disloyalty is close kin to cowardice, refers the pollution to those defiled by the impurities of emperor-worship, and counts eight epithets in all. Ellicott divides the word for fear, since there is a high and holy fear in which the Christian passes his sojourn here and a base and selfish fear of man which brings a snare, and finds the characters arranged in four pairs.

outliers.note: Notes that among those admitted to the city are men who have sinned through fear and faithlessness, so that it is sin unrepented of, not sin committed, which shuts a man out.

themes: the cowardly and the faithless heading the list
their part in the lake that burneth with fire and brimstone, which is the second death
sin loved and unrepented of is what closes the gate

9.pericope_label: Come, I will show thee the bride, the Lamb's wife; and he carried me away in the spirit

schools.summary: Gill says John was in an ecstasy, so that it only seemed to him as if he were taken from place to place, none of these visions being corporeal sights but things represented to his spirit, as with Paul caught up to the third heaven, who could not tell whether he was in the body or out of it; he notes that the Ethiopic version makes the Spirit the agent, not the evil spirit who once carried our Lord bodily to an exceeding high mountain.

Henry generalises from the choice of messenger, that God has a variety of work for his holy angels: sometimes to sound the trumpet of divine providence and give fair warning to a careless world, sometimes to pour out the vials of his anger upon impenitent sinners, and sometimes to discover things of a heavenly nature to the heirs of salvation. He reads the subject as the church in her perfect state, comely through the comeliness put upon her by her husband, and draws a rule from the vantage point, that those who would have clear views of heaven must get as near heaven as they can, into the mount of vision, whence, as from the top of Pisgah, they may behold the goodly land.

Clarke keeps to the practical use of the height, since being above the city he might see every street and lane of it. Wesley notes that the same angel had before showed him Babylon, which is directly opposed to the new Jerusalem, compares Ezekiel's holy city, which agrees in many particulars but differs in more since the prophet describes a temple and John saw none, observes that the old city is now so forgotten that this one is called simply Jerusalem, and adds how St John longed to enter in, though the time was not yet come.

Ellicott notes that one of the angels which had the vials of wrath had shown the seer the guilty Babylon and that one of the same company now shows him the pure Bride, and will not stop at the view-ground, since the glimpse of God's coming glories is best gained from the consecrated heights of self-surrender and prayer; he sets the scene beside the temptation, where the tempter showed our Lord the kingdoms of the world while the comforting angel shows the prophet the city which hath the foundations. Robertson makes the same point of the introduction, which repeats the announcement about the harlot city word for word, and thinks the mountain cannot be Zion since the new Jerusalem is seen descending from it. Barnes cannot say why one of these angels was employed, but suggests it was fitting that those who had brought destruction on the enemies of the church should announce her triumph.

themes: the bride, the Lamb’s wife, set against the harlot city
he carried me away in the spirit to a mountain great and high
the descriptions of Ezekiel and of John compared

11.pericope_label: Having the glory of God: a wall great and high, and twelve gates

schools.summary: Gill takes the glory two ways at once, as resting on the saints themselves, whose bodies will be made like Christ's glorious body, and as meaning the presence of God, the Shechinah that filled tabernacle and temple; if the faces of Moses and Stephen shone so brightly at that presence, how much more shall the saints shine. On the wall he canvasses the interpretations, rejecting the Spirit of God and the eternal decree, allowing that many take it for the doctrine of the gospel, and settling on the almighty power of God.

Clarke describes the stone by its optics, since among precious stones some of the same species are far more valuable, their worth being in proportion as they are free from flaws and of a good water, and the stone here is a jasper perfectly transparent; the light of the city is intense and splendid but tinged with green to make it agreeable to the sight, nothing being so friendly to the eye as blue or green. He reports a rabbinic parallel from the Sohar, that in the palace of the world to come there are twelve gates inscribed with the names of the tribes, and that he who is of the tribe of Reuben is received at none but his own. Wesley presses the figure of the window and makes it a single one running round the city, so that the light does not come in from without but shines out from within to a great distance.

Robertson calls the brightness a luminary, a word found in the New Testament only here and where Paul bids Christians shine as lights, quotes Swete that the luminary of the Holy City is her witness to Christ, and notes that the word for gate is used through this book for the gate tower rather than the door. Barnes traces the same word to its ordinary use, where it means a light-giver and in profane writers commonly a window, adds that the jasper is essentially a quartz so that the word crystal shows which sort is meant, and gives the angels at the gates the duty of watching that the great enemy should not make an insidious approach as he did to the earthly Paradise. Ellicott agrees that the glory is the true Shechinah, and finds the city lustrous as the diamond but shot with the green tint of the emerald bow which swept the throne.

themes: her light like a stone most precious, clear as crystal
a wall great and high, with twelve gates and twelve angels
three gates on each of the four sides

14.pericope_label: Twelve foundations bearing the apostles' names; the city lieth foursquare

schools.summary: Gill keeps the doctrine straight before counting stones, since Christ is the one and only foundation and the twelve are named only because he was ministerially laid by the twelve apostles; the plural also marks the firm state of a church which is a city that has foundations.

Clarke supposes twelve stones, one serving as threshold to each gate, to intimate that souls enter the Church by the doctrine of the apostles, notes that several excellent manuscripts make the reed explicitly a measuring rod, and finds the quadrangular form a token of perfection and stability, the square being among the Greeks a figure of perfection so that the square man was one of unsullied integrity. Wesley reads the foundations as showing that the inhabitants built only on the faith once delivered to the saints, measures the city against Jerusalem and Babylon and asks what inconsiderable villages these were by comparison, and warns that a deep reverence is necessary in treating such things, that we may neither understand them too literally and grossly nor go too far from the natural force of the words.

Ellicott sees the whole Church of both Testaments in the city with the apostles' work specially recognised, in complete harmony with what Paul writes to the Ephesians, and turns aside to the objection that John could not have written a book which reckons the apostles among the foundations, since the same argument would tell against Paul's authorship of Ephesians. He contrasts the golden reed with the reed of an earlier chapter, whose measuring symbolised preservation amid danger, whereas this exhibits the beauty and proportion of a city dwelling at peace, and is brisk with those who are nervously anxious about the monstrous appearance of such a city. Robertson observes that all twelve names are written and not Peter's only, wonders whether the name on the twelfth stone is Judas or Matthias, and notes that the city is a perfect cube like the holy of holies in Solomon's temple. Barnes prefers twelve courses laid one above another to twelve stones set at intervals, and explains that the height of three hundred and seventy-five miles precludes any literal city in Palestine.

positions.position: twelve courses of stone laid one above another beneath the wall
twelve stones, one serving as the threshold of each gate

themes: the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb in the foundations
a golden reed to measure the city, and the gates, and the wall
the length and the breadth and the height of it are equal

17.pericope_label: The wall an hundred and forty and four cubits, of jasper, and the city pure gold

schools.summary: Gill takes the number back to its root, since twelve times twelve is a hundred and forty-four, a number mystical and apostolical and suited to the perfect state of this church, whence the twelve gates and their angels and the twelve foundations; and he makes the jasper expressive of the impregnableness and duration and brightness of salvation by Christ.

Clarke explains the unit, the cubit being named from the elbow and reaching to the tip of the middle finger, generally reckoned at a foot and a half though the pyramids suggest twenty-one inches, and offers an arithmetical conceit, that twenty-four, the number of tribes and apostles together, multiplied by a six-foot rod gives precisely a hundred and forty-four. He confirms that the oriental jasper is almost indestructible, then turns on the popular use of the passage, which has been most injudiciously applied to heaven so that we hear of golden walls and pavements without considering that nothing of this was intended literally, and that gold and jewels can have no place in a spiritual world; in symbols they are proper, but construed into realities they are very improper. Wesley states the arrangement plainly, that the wall was built of jasper and the houses were of pure gold.

Robertson notes another multiple of twelve and is not sure whether height or breadth is meant, reckons two hundred and sixteen feet against the fifteen hundred miles of the city, puts the qualifying clause in Bengel's phrase as man's measure which is angel's, and adds that the city shone like a mass of gold against the jasper lustre of the wall. Barnes compares the walls of Babylon, which Herodotus put at three hundred and fifty feet, so that this height gives every proper idea of security while the city towers immensely above it, and says the human standard is named to prevent mistake, since an angel is measuring. Ellicott presses the doubleness of that clause, since the measure is true for men and true for angels, and while it may mean only that the angel used the ordinary standard it may imply that the vision is true for all; it is figurative, he says, but not mere figure.

outliers.note: Takes the gold from Lange as referring to the sun and so to the manifestation of God's love, and reads the wealth of heaven as love: no motive of self-interest dims its lustre, so the gold is clear as glass.

themes: the measure of a man, that is, of the angel
the building of the wall was of jasper, and the city was pure gold
whether such descriptions may be preached as literal

19.pericope_label: The foundations garnished with all manner of precious stones

schools.summary: Gill rules out several readings: the sense is not that every foundation held all manner of stones but that each had its own; the stones are not to be applied to the persons of the apostles, who were not the foundations but only had their names written on them; and still less will he allow Brightman's fancy that they mean ministers of the latter day who shall convert the Jews in the countries where these stones are found.

Clarke takes the foundations for the thresholds of the gates and reads the arrangement as a scheme of the two dispensations, the gates being the twelve tribes and the thresholds the twelve apostles, so that there is no entrance but through those gates and none but over these thresholds; the Mosaic dispensation was the preparation for the gospel, which without it would have no original. He and Wesley give the shades of the stones, the sardonyx red streaked with white, the sardius a deep blood red, the chrysolite dusky green with a cast of yellow, the topaz pale yellow and the amethyst violet; and Wesley recalls that the same stones on the high priest's breastplate were an emblem of the happiness of God's church in his presence, adding that here each stone is not the ornament of a foundation but the foundation.

Barnes traces several names to their origins, the chalcedony from a town opposite Byzantium, the topaz from an island in the Arabian Gulf, the chrysoprasus from the words for gold and a leek, and the amethyst from a word meaning not to be intoxicated, the gem having been thought an antidote against drunkenness. Robertson denies that the list carries any necessary mystical meaning, quoting Moffatt that the writer is simply trying to convey the impression of a radiant and superb structure, calls Charles's identification of the stones with the signs of the zodiac a needless performance, sorts the whole list by Swete into four families of colour, and will entertain Clement of Alexandria's suggestion that the variety illustrates the variety of gifts in the twelve apostles. Ellicott sets the adorned Bride against the harlot whose robe was decked with gold and pearls, hears in the diversity the doctrine of gifts differing while the Lord is the same, and sees the stones, ranged by shades of colour rather than by the order of the breastplate, encircling the city as with a rainbow belt.

themes: every precious stone in the foundations of the wall
harmony, not monotony; variety, not sameness; unity, not uniformity
whether the twelve stones carry a mystical meaning

21.pericope_label: The twelve gates were twelve pearls; and I saw no temple therein

schools.summary: Gill reads the pearls as a double emblem, of the preciousness of Christ by whom the saints enter and of the saints who enter by him, and lists what the city lacks: no material temple as in the old Jerusalem, none such as Ezekiel described, and no place of public worship as under the gospel, since there will be no preaching or administering of ordinances in that state; the Jews expect a third temple, he adds, but in vain.

Henry says that perfect and direct communion with God will more than supply the place of gospel institutions, and asks what words could more fully express the union and co-equality of the Son with the Father.

Clarke says plainly that it is out of the order of nature to produce a pearl large enough for a gate to such a city, and tells the rabbinic story of the disciple who laughed at his master for teaching that God would provide gems thirty cubits every way for those gates, and who afterwards, at sea, saw the ministering angels cutting gems and was told they were for the gates of Jerusalem; on the temple he gives the reason in a line, that there was no need of one where God and the Lamb were manifestly present. Wesley states the presence rather than the loss, that God fills the new heaven and the new earth, surrounds the city and sanctifies all that are in it, and is all in all.

Ellicott finds a doctrine in the contrast, since the foundations are diverse and the gates alike, so that there is one way though many roads; the pearl was reckoned the most valuable of stones among the ancients and is a fit emblem of the highest truth, and it is the only precious stone the art of man cannot improve, since the artificer may give fresh lustre to emerald and sapphire but must lift no tool upon the pearl. On the missing temple he draws out what it implies, since the age of the Church triumphing succeeds the age of the Church toiling and the external helps required for edifying the body of Christ are no longer needed: tongues and prophecies and knowledge may pass away, churches disappear into the one glorious Church, and every merely local aspect of worship is at an end. Barnes turns the absence into a positive, since the city was all temple and nothing but a temple, with worship ascending from every part. Robertson makes the same point as a reversal, since where the apostle elsewhere calls us the sanctuary of God, here God is our sanctuary, and so is the Lamb.

themes: every several gate was of one pearl
the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass
the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it

23.pericope_label: The city had no need of the sun; the nations shall walk in the light of it

schools.summary: Gill allows the clause a literal sense, since the luminaries every earthly city needs may still be in being without having the use they now have, and cites the Jewish saying that the orb of the sun belongs to this world and not to the future state; on the nations he will not have all the nations of the world meant, since all will not be saved, nor the Gentiles only, but all the elect called out of every nation. He takes the open gates for the safety of the inhabitants rather than free traffic between the risen and the living, since they will have no enemy to fear.

Clarke reports the Jewish tradition that in the world to come the Israelites shall have no need of the sun by day nor the moon by night, and adds that God's light shines in this city and is concentrated in the Lamb, from whom it is everywhere diffused; the open gates he reads of the present Church, which stands ever open to receive sinners of all sorts and degrees and nations. Wesley says the glory is infinitely brighter than the sun, and qualifies the glory the kings bring, since it is not their old glory, which is now abolished, but such as becomes the new earth and receives an immense addition by their entrance.

Robertson puts it as a comparison of brightness, since if sun and moon did shine they would add no light in the presence of the Shekinah Glory, and prefers Swete's view of Christ as the one lamp over against the many lampstands of the churches on earth; on the nations he reports Swete's uncertainty whether this is a picture of heaven itself or of some purpose of God towards humanity not yet revealed. Ellicott notices that the emblem of the Lamb recurs here, so that the memory of Christ's work on earth is never obliterated and gives depth to the city's joy, follows the best manuscripts in dropping the qualifying words about the saved, and sets the vision against the writer's circumstances, since the prophet looks out from the loneliness of churches then persecuted and sees her enlarged and honoured. Barnes takes the glory brought in to mean whatever the kings reckon their glory, and reads the open gates as meaning that the dwellers there are not prisoners, the universe being open to them.

outliers.note: Takes the absence of night as more than physical, meaning nothing of which night is the emblem: no calamity, no bereavement, no windows darkened for the loss of friends.

themes: the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof
the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honour into it
the gates shall not be shut at all by day, for there shall be no night there

26.pericope_label: There shall in no wise enter into it anything that defileth

schools.summary: Gill reads the glory of the nations as the people of God themselves, who though reckoned the filth of the world are the excellent in the earth, and who will be presented to the King by rulers who had been their fathers and protectors; he adds a second sense, that whatever is great among the nations will count as nothing beside this state. On the exclusion he takes the defilement to be evil thoughts and words and actions, notes the variant readings of the versions, and finds an allusion to the temple into which no unclean person might come, so that neither the profane sinner nor the self-righteous man whose righteousness is filthy rags may enter, but only those washed in the blood of Christ.

Clarke keeps the prophetic background in view, the promise being that the Gentiles should contribute their gifts to the riches and glory of the temple, and turns the exclusion on the reader: he defines the impure man as one who turns the grace of God into lasciviousness and the liar as one who holds and propagates false doctrines, reminds every Christian that his baptism bound him to renounce the devil and all his works, and asks whether the reader is of that number or is expecting an eternal glory while living in sin, since presuming on the mercy of God is as ruinous as despairing of his grace. Wesley supposes a select part of each nation is meant, so that everything which can make the city honourable shall be found in it, and closes on the register, since the blessedness belongs to true and holy and persevering believers.

Robertson makes the comparison with the city already fallen, since Rome gathered the merchandise of the world whereas the City of God will have the best of all the nations, and leaves standing the question these recurrent glimpses raise, whether John runs parallel pictures of heaven and hell after the judgment or whether, as Charles puts it, the unclean are still on earth and cannot enter though the gates stand open; in apocalyptic writing, he adds, literalism and chronology cannot be insisted on. Barnes states the sum in a sentence, that the blessed world will be made up of all that was truly valuable and pure on the earth, and points out that the word is literally anything common, the negative being of the strongest kind. Ellicott sets the exclusion beside the open gates, which stand open always and yet admit no evil thing, and traces the allusion to the care of the Jews in keeping every unclean thing from the sanctuary.

themes: they shall bring the glory and honour of the nations into it
nothing common, nor he that worketh abomination and a lie
but they which are written in the Lamb’s book of life
